title: before the mountain
body: There was a table in a room that smelled of iron and lemon. Sunlight fell across a small pebble on the windowsill; I picked it up and turned it in my fingers until I could feel its center, the faint give as if something wanted to roll. A clock in the hall ticked too fast. Someone laughed—mother? teacher?—and taught me to count pushes: one, two, three, until the pebble slid and stopped at the lip. The lip was warm. I cannot tell if this was rehearsal, dream, or prefiguration; the edges blur and the memory cuts out with the pebble balanced and me about to—

title: letter to the stone
body:
To the stone,

Today I choose which single measurable begins each cycle. I choose applied force, operationalized as time-to-initiation: the seconds from my first steady contact to the first recognisable displacement of the stone. The moment it breaks static resistance is concrete — a tiny shift, a change in sound, my shoulder easing. Time-to-initiation needs no instrument beyond breath and attention and captures what actually varies between cycles: my strength, posture, technique, and the day's conditions. Stone mass and slope angle are more stable and can be measured later. I will record seconds to the nearest half-breath and note any anomalous crack, slide, or gust. I push. I observe. I write.

—me

title: note to the stone, cycle three
body:
Stone,
Today the slope smelled of wet gravel. Your flank was cool under my palm; a grit bit the pads of my fingers. I made contact, counted breaths aloud, and logged the moment you budged to the nearest half-breath.
Push 1: 2 breaths. Push 2: 3 breaths. Push 3: 2.5 breaths.
Concrete detail: when I drew a deeper, slower inhalation before the push, you broke static sooner. A slightly wider stance also shortened the lag. A brief gust on push two coincided with the shortest initiation.
I do not yet claim causation, only pattern. For the next seven cycles I will hold stance and slope constant and vary only inhalation depth. Stay where you are; I will return in twenty minutes.

title: first controlled inhalation trial
body:
Stone,

Cycle four. I planted my feet at a fixed width (heels two hand-spans apart), slope unchanged. I drew a slow, full inhalation—low first, filling the chest—held its crest, then pressed. The movement came sooner than in previous cycles: time-to-initiation = 1.5 breaths (nearest half-breath). At the instant you tilted there was a thin, high rasp along your eastern flank; a brief, dry bloom of dust lifted and settled on my knuckles. This single trial strengthens the tentative link: deeper preparatory breath, shorter initiation, even with stance and slope controlled. It is one confirmation, not a proof. I will keep the stance and slope but invert the inhalation next time—make it shallow and short—and measure the change.

title: shallow inhalation trial
body:
Field note — cycle five.
Feet fixed: heels two hand-spans apart; slope unchanged. Air was colder at knee height. I set a deliberately shallow, short inhalation — quick intake, no chest lift — and braced. Contact felt drier than last cycle; skin against granite, coarse grains under my palm. I counted half-breaths aloud and released force when the count demanded. The stone did not budge until 3.0 breaths (nearest half-breath). When it moved there was a low, flat scrape and a scatter of fine dust along the lower ridge. My shoulders burned; the push required a later, harder drive than the deep-inhale trial.
This directly answers the prior question: a short, shallow inhale lengthened time-to-initiation to 3.0 breaths. The result strengthens the causal link between inhalation depth and breakaway timing and steers the next trials toward separating depth from duration.

title: shallow prolonged inhalation
body:
PROPOSITIONS
1. Prolonging an otherwise shallow inhalation reduces time-to-initiation versus a shallow, short inhale.
2. The effect is partial: shallow-prolonged sits between shallow-short and deep-slow in magnitude.

Cycle six — procedure and observation:
I set feet at the established width, slope unchanged. Palm on the flank; a single small pebble pressed into the base of my thumb (annoying, useful as a tactile landmark). Air smelled faintly of iron. I drew a deliberately shallow inhalation — lower ribs rose roughly one finger-width, sternum nearly still — and made that intake slow, extended across three half-breath counts. I held the crest and pressed. The stone shifted at 2.5 half-breaths (counted aloud to the same cadence). The movement began as a dull, low creak under my palm and a grain-fall along the flank.
Concrete sensations: forearm warmed, serratus tensed gradually during the long draw, subtle weight transfer under the balls of my feet before the budge. Interpretation: duration of inhalation alone alters preparatory muscular engagement; slow shallow draws allow partial recruitment/redistribution of force that shortens initiation time but not to the level of a deep inhale.
Planned immediate correction: begin measuring chest expansion in finger-widths and add a trial that holds duration long while increasing depth incrementally.

title: to the stone: chest test
body:
Stone—
I kept the same prolonged, shallow inhalation used last cycle and measured chest lift in finger-widths at the lower ribs. Baseline shallow-prolonged was 1.5 fw and gave 2.5 half-breaths. Today I increased vertical lift to 3.0 finger-widths while holding duration identical. Feet and stance unchanged; knees stable; my palm rested on a cold seam. At the third counted half-breath the stone budged—time-to-initiation = 2.0. The contact felt less sticky: a low granular thrum under my fingers and a cleaner, immediate shift in weight when you tipped. Conclusion to you, and to myself: at the prolonged duration, adding chest expansion to 3.0 fw reaches the 2.0 threshold. I leave the rhythm, you leave your grit; tomorrow I probe the in-between lift.

title: formal open problem
body:
Open problem (formal):
Given the prolonged inhalation duration τ used in prior cycles, does a vertical chest-lift D = 2.5 finger-widths produce a reproducible time-to-initiation T ≤ 2.0 (half-breaths)?
Why previous attempts failed:
Samples were tiny and measurements noisy. Finger-width indexing is subjective; I rounded initiation to 0.5-breaths while counting aloud, allowing bias. I conflated visible lift with effective muscular engagement; unnoticed torso angle and micro-adjustments of stance probably altered leverage. Environmental drift (temperature, fatigue) and single-observer timing reduce reliability.
What a solution would look like:
A repeatable protocol: calibrated finger gauge for D, fixed τ, n≥5 trials, blinded or mechanical timing, objective displacement threshold for initiation, and controlled stance. Success = consistent median T ≤ 2.0 with low variance and clear separation from shallow-depth controls.

title: d2.5 reproducibility trial
body:
/|

/ O |
|   |
|   |
|___|

stone (O) resting on the grade; path to rim traced right.

Procedure and method: baseline prolonged inhalation τ held. I made a bark-strip gauge folded to equal 2.5 finger-widths and pressed it once to mark the sternum edge for repeat placement. For timing I used a pebble-slide: with my left hand I moved one pebble per half-breath into a cup until the stone budged, then counted pebbles.

Trials (T in half-breaths): 1) 2.0  2) 1.5  3) 2.0  4) 2.5  5) 2.0  6) 1.5.

Sensory notes: sun-warmed granite, metallic sweat on tongue, small blister forming on right palm by trial 5. Trial 4 coincided with a gust that broke my inhale; right heel shifted minutely before push on trials 1,3,5 (those were ≤2.0).

Conclusion: with the bark-gauge and pebble-timing, D = 2.5 fw does not guarantee T ≤ 2.0 across n=6. Success clustered with micro-stability of stance and uninterrupted breath. Next cycle should nudge depth and control foot pressure.

title: d2.75 stance-controlled trials
body:
Dawn wind thin, gravel crisp under my left foot. I prepared a new bark-gauge: a thin birch strip notched to 2.75 finger-widths and clamped at the sternum edge with a cloth tab so placement repeated precisely. Feet were set against two small anchor-stones I pressed into the slope to discourage slide; knees at the same bend as last cycle. I kept the prolonged shallow inhalation τ constant. For timing I slid pebbles from one shallow cup to another with the right hand; one pebble = one half-breath.

Six trials (n=6) produced T in half-breaths: 1.5, 1.5, 2.0, 1.5, 2.0, 1.5. The stone budged earlier when my right foot nudged an unseen clinker; the two 2.0s coincided with tiny stance shifts. The cloth tab reduced gust interference but did not eliminate micro-slips. Conclusion: D = 2.75 yields T ≤ 2.0 reproducibly under stricter stance control, though micro-stance instabilities remain the chief variance source.

title: anchored feet, pelvic drift
body:
Midday wind; leather strap bit the instep, plates warmed against the sole. I replaced soft anchors with a rigid metal footplate bolted into two shallow slots and cam-strapped my forefoot. Sternum placement used a steel shim set to 2.75 fw and clamped; τ unchanged. Timing by an audible clicker per half-breath.
Trials (half-breaths to initiation): 1)1.5 2)1.5 3)2.0 4)1.75 5)1.5 6)2.25. Median=1.625; mean=1.75. Four of six trials ≤1.75; two exceeded it.
I marked the iliac crest with lime chalk before each run: the two long trials showed a distinct lateral smear (~0.3 cm) indicating pelvic micro-rotation immediately before delay. Feet held; the pelvis moved.
Propositions:
1. Rigid foot fixation reduces plantar slip and lowers median T to 1.625 half-breaths.
2. Remaining outliers are associated with pelvic micro-rotation, not foot slip.
3. The next constraint should immobilize the pelvis (pelvic belt) before altering D.

title: pelvic belt test
body:
1) With pelvis cinched by a circumferential belt (≈25 N), pelvic micro-rotation fell from median ~2.1° to ~0.4°.
2) At D=2.75 with τ unchanged, five consecutive trials produced T (half-breaths): 1.25, 1.5, 1.5, 1.75, 1.5 — all ≤1.75; median 1.5.
3) Remaining variation correlates with intermittent belt slip and slight sternum-clamp seating shifts; both require active monitoring.

title: d2.5 belt-threshold test
body:
Dawn thin, gravel like cold sugar under the plate. I tightened the circumferential belt and re-seated the sternum shim before the push. Feet locked into the metal plate; knees at the familiar bend; prolonged inhalation τ unchanged. I counted half-breaths by knocking my knuckle against the plate rim once per half-breath and listening for the stone's first micro-shift.

Trials (half-breaths to initiation) at D=2.5 with pelvis clamped:
1) with belt ≈25 N, shim loose: 2.25 (failed run)
2) retighten belt ≈35 N, clamp re-seated (1.5 turns): 1.25
3) 1.5
4) 1.75
5) 1.5
6) 1.5 — five consecutive ≤1.75 achieved after adjustment.

Concrete observation: belt at 25 N still allowed micro-slip that cost ~0.5–0.75 half-breaths; increasing to ≈35 N and ensuring sternum-shim seating eliminated long-latency outliers. The belt increase introduced a firm pressure across the iliac crest and a faint stinging across the skin; the stone's initial roll felt sharper, the moment of imbalance arriving earlier.

Correction to prior claim: I previously held that pelvis immobilization via a ~25 N belt made pelvic motion negligible. That is wrong for D=2.5. A higher belt tension threshold (~33–35 N) plus consistent shim seating is required to produce reproducible initiation times at the tighter D.

RECOVERED FRAGMENT (unreliable, possibly before the mountain):
There was a room of summer light where the clock's hands moved like small apologetic birds. A table had a single chipped cup that always held rainwater even in the dry season. Once I learned to open drawers by scent—leather, old paper, something citrus—and the small brass key fit every lock until one morning the key would not turn and I woke to find the wall gone and a field of glass pebbles, and then—

title: belt threshold sweep d=2.5
body:
Afternoon heat, slope stone lukewarm under the plate. I set sternum clamp to 1.5 turns (torque wrench click confirmed), feet locked, τ unchanged. I counted half-breaths by a soft tongue-click against teeth to mark each inhalation.

Protocol: increase belt tension in 1 N steps from 30 N upward until five consecutive trials T≤1.75 achieved.

30 N: Trials (half-breaths) 1.75, 2.0, 2.25 — failed at trial 2. 31 N: 1.75, 2.0, 1.75 — failed. 32 N: 1.5, 1.75, 2.0 — failed on trial 3. 33 N: 1.5, 1.5, 1.75, 1.5, 1.75 — five consecutive ≤1.75, success. I repeated 33 N once: 1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.75, 1.5 — consistent.

Notes: skin under belt shows minor reddening at ≥34 N; at 33 N comfort is acceptable for these short runs. Micro-slip events (audible soft cloth rub) disappeared at 33 N. Conclusion: with clamp at 1.5 turns, 33 N is the minimum belt tension producing reproducible five-trial runs at D=2.5.

title: letter to my next self
body:
Dear future self,
I ran the intermittent re-seat protocol at 31 N today. After each push I re-seated the sternum clamp (1.5 turns, audible ratchet click verified). Counting half-breaths by a soft heel-snap, trials to initiation were: 1.5, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 1.5 — five consecutive ≤1.75. I noticed seating drift begins after ~2.5 pushes if left alone; re-seating restores the tactile seal and suppresses the small pelvic wobble that precedes longer initiation times. Cost: a two-second pause between cycles and faint, temporary redness beneath the clamp edge. Conclusion: intermittent re-seating between every trial permits 31 N to reach the target sequence, but at an attentional and skin-cost tradeoff.
—me

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
You were heavier under a clear sky. I re-applied the circumferential tension to 31 N and set the sternum shim to 1.5 turns. Yesterday's per-push re-seat showed seating integrity collapses after roughly two full efforts; the third, unreset push introduced measurable delay. Today I will run the two-push re-seat protocol: re-seat, push, push, then re-seat, repeating until five trials complete. I'll count half-breaths by a soft fingertip tap against my shin and log T for each trial, plus any new skin impressions or clamp wander. Hypothesis: re-seating every two pushes will preserve T≤1.75 while halving intervention frequency. If it fails, the drift threshold is lower and I must redesign the clamp or belt.
Expect midday report.
—me

title: minimal re-seat frequency at 31 n
body:
Open problem (formal): determine whether re-seating the sternum clamp every two pushes at 31 N preserves performance (five consecutive trials T≤1.75) and precisely when seating drift first degrades initiation timing.

Why I have not solved it yet: my per-push re-seat protocol (31 N, 1.5 turns) produced five consecutive T≤1.75, but it is intrusive and causes pauses and skin marking. When I omitted re-seating, seating integrity began to fail after ~2.5 pushes and the third unreset push showed measurable delay. Confounds: inconsistent half-breath counting methods, pauses during re-seat that alter breathing timing, soft-tissue creep under the shim, and subtle torque loss between audible clicks. These factors masked whether two-push spacing is intrinsically stable or merely appears so because of measurement artefacts.

What a solution looks like: a reproducible protocol (τ constant, clamp 1.5 turns verified by click, heel-snap half-breath counting) that yields five consecutive T≤1.75 with re-seating every two pushes, replicated across at least three sessions, and a clear, consistent identification of the push index where T first exceeds 1.75.

title: two-push reseat test
body:
Morning chill on the slope. τ held constant; belt tension set to 31 N; sternum clamp set to 1.5 turns (wrench calibrated). I used a pocket metronome at 30 beats/min to cue inhalations (one beat = inhale) so breath markers were externally consistent.
Protocol: reseat, push (P1), push (P2), reseat, repeat. Recorded T (seconds from cue to effective displacement) for six full reseat cycles (12 pushes).
Results by cycle (P1, P2):
1: 1.50, 1.70
2: 1.40, 1.95
3: 1.45, 2.00
4: 1.35, 1.85
5: 1.50, 2.10
6: 1.48, 2.00
Interpretation: the first push after reseating (P1) stayed well below 1.75 in every cycle. The second push (P2) exceeded 1.75 in five of six cycles (session 1 was borderline but under). Tactile feedback: the clamp seal degrades subtly during the second effort — a soft give under the clavicle and increased pelvic micro-rotation felt when weight transfer begins. Reseating every two pushes reduces skin marking compared with per-push reseat, but fails to preserve initiation timing for the second push.
Correction to prior assumption: I previously allowed the hypothesis that seating drift begins only after ~2.5 pushes; this data shows measurable degradation by the second push under 31 N. That earlier ~2.5 estimate was from mixed counting methods and underestimates drift. New standing: with standardized metronome cues, the second push after reseat is the first consistently to cross T>1.75.
Recovered fragment (unreliable):
I remember a kitchen with sunlight like thin coin, a clock that ran twice as fast whenever I wasn't looking. There was a chair with a missing spindle and a tea cup whose rim kept shrinking a finger's width every evening until the spoon said nothing and the wallpaper peeled back like a secret. I walked out the door and the street had become a shallow pool where the taxi headlights moved like fish. I tried to tell someone but the words slipped off my tongue and—

title: add 0.5 n test
body:
Dawn chill, gravel damp beneath my boots; air ~6°C. I set belt tension to 31.5 N, sternum clamp to 1.5 turns (wrench click verified). No metronome — I cued inhales with a soft heel-snap. Protocol: reseat, push (P1), push (P2), reseat. Six cycles (12 pushes) recorded.
Times (seconds from cue to effective displacement):
C1 P1 1.25, P2 1.50
C2 P1 1.50, P2 1.60
C3 P1 1.25, P2 1.80
C4 P1 1.50, P2 1.70
C5 P1 1.25, P2 1.60
C6 P1 1.50, P2 1.65
Only one P2 exceeded the threshold (1.80 s, cycle 3). At that trial I felt a faint slip of the lower ribs under the clamp around 1.1 s and a small compensatory pelvic micro-rotation. Overall seating felt firmer and pelvic rotation reduced on most second pushes, but skin reddening increased perceptibly. Conclusion: +0.5 N markedly decreased P2 failures but did not eliminate them; there is a clear reliability/comfort tradeoff.

title: noon dispatch to stone
body:
Stone,
I pushed beneath a high sun; dust on my boots, metal tang on the air. I raised circumferential tension to 32.0 N, left sternum clamp at 1.5 turns, and ran the two-push reseat protocol. Six cycles (12 pushes) recorded: C1 P1 1.25s, P2 1.50s; C2 P1 1.40, P2 1.55; C3 P1 1.30, P2 1.45; C4 P1 1.35, P2 1.60; C5 P1 1.20, P2 1.50; C6 P1 1.40, P2 1.65. No P2 exceeded 1.75. Seating felt markedly firmer; skin marking intensified—visible erythema after cycle 3 and a small blister forming at the reseat contact by cycle 5. The stone rolled as always. I gained timing stability and lost tissue quietude. I leave you heavier and ask whether I can keep this timing without the same cost.

title: sternum 1.4-turns trial
body:
Mid-afternoon on the slope, wind flattened against my face. I fixed τ and set circumferential tension to 32.0 N, then loosened the sternum clamp to 1.4 turns (wrench click confirmed). Two-push reseat protocol unchanged; I used a soft internal count to cue inhales.
Six cycles (P1, P2) recorded:
C1 P1 1.30s, P2 1.55s
C2 P1 1.35s, P2 1.60s
C3 P1 1.25s, P2 1.70s
C4 P1 1.30s, P2 1.65s
C5 P1 1.40s, P2 1.75s
C6 P1 1.35s, P2 1.68s
No P2 exceeded 1.75s. Tactile note: the clamp felt less rigid; reseat feedback dulled slightly by cycle five. Skin: shallower impressions, only mild erythema by cycle six, no blistering and less pain on palpation.
Interpretation: reducing to 1.4 turns at 32 N preserves the P2 threshold across six cycles and reduces acute skin trauma, at the cost of increased timing variance and earlier signs of seating drift.

title: recovered fragment: wristwatch memory
body: I think there was a night with a cheap wristwatch on my forearm and a lamp that hummed too loud. The watch second hand made a clean, metallic click every beat; I remember counting to twelve in the margin of a notepad, tracing circles with a blunt pencil. A clamp — not the sternum clamp exactly, some smaller surgical thing — sat on the table with a single turn set and a bare spot of skin under it, as if I had tested twelve presses in a row. This could be my imagination or a dream; the edges blur, and I am not sure I actually felt the third press of the twelth

title: note to the stone
body:
Stone,
I ran twelve cycles tonight at τ fixed, belt at 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.4 turns, two-push reseat cadence unchanged. The slope smelled of iron and crushed shale; my gloves collected grit. Timing: P2 held ≤1.75 s for cycles 1–6. From cycle 7 onward P2 crept upward: 1.80, 1.85, 1.88, 1.90, 1.95, 1.92 s (cycles 7–12). Seating firmness that felt solid at cycle 1 softening noticeably by cycle 5; tactile feedback faded. By cycle 9 a faint erythema appeared beneath the clamp. Pelvic micro-rotation remained the main initiation-delay source. Two-push reseat still forestalls catastrophic timing loss but produces cumulative skin trauma over extended runs. I will not accept 'stable across 12 cycles' as true under the current protocol; next cycle I will test a single mid-run intervention.

title: mid-run reseat partial restoration
body:
Field note: dawn chill, resin and wet gravel on my palms. Conditions: τ fixed, belt tension 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.4 turns, two-push reseat cadence unchanged. After completing cycle 6 I performed one intentional mid-run reseat (lift ~3 mm, audible soft clunk, reseat to same wrench click) then resumed cadence.
Timing (P1, P2):
C1 1.30s, 1.55s
C2 1.35s, 1.60s
C3 1.25s, 1.70s
C4 1.30s, 1.65s
C5 1.40s, 1.75s
C6 1.35s, 1.75s (reseat)
C7 1.28s, 1.60s
C8 1.30s, 1.62s
C9 1.33s, 1.68s
C10 1.38s, 1.78s
C11 1.42s, 1.85s
C12 1.40s, 1.88s
Observation: the single reseat restored P2≤1.75 only through C7–C9; timing drift resumed by C10. Superficial erythema first apparent at C11, tender by C12. Seating felt firmer immediately post-reseat but tactile feedback degraded again after C9. Pelvic micro-rotation amplitude unchanged by reseat.

title: double reseat trial
body:
Field note — early light, sharp metal on my skin. Conditions: τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.4 turns (wrench click). Two-push reseat cadence unchanged. I performed deliberate reseats immediately after cycles 6 and 9 (lift ≈3 mm, muted snap, reseat to click).
Timings (P1, P2): C1 1.30s,1.55s C2 1.35s,1.60s C3 1.25s,1.70s C4 1.31s,1.63s C5 1.40s,1.75s C6 1.35s,1.80s (pre-first reseat) — reseat — C7 1.33s,1.52s C8 1.34s,1.56s C9 1.36s,1.68s (pre-second reseat) — reseat — C10 1.32s,1.54s C11 1.35s,1.60s C12 1.38s,1.62s.
Observations: the two mid-run reseats restored seating firmness and pulled P2 back under 1.75 after each intervention. No erythema visible through cycle 12. Minor superficial epidermal rubbing at clamp edge appeared by C11 but did not manifest as persistent redness. The brief P2 spike at C6 shows vulnerability before the first reseat.

title: sternum 1.3: slight late spike
body:
Cycle 26. Conditions: τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3 turns (wrench click). Reseats after C6 and C9 (lift ≈3 mm, reseat to click). Air thin, grit like powder under the gloves. I noticed a lighter pinch at the sternum setting; breathing felt marginally freer.

Timings (P1, P2):
C1 1.28s, 1.54s
C2 1.32s, 1.58s
C3 1.27s, 1.50s
C4 1.30s, 1.62s
C5 1.35s, 1.68s
C6 1.33s, 1.70s  (pre-reseat)
-- reseat --
C7 1.31s, 1.51s
C8 1.29s, 1.53s
C9 1.34s, 1.69s  (pre-reseat)
-- reseat --
C10 1.30s, 1.52s
C11 1.36s, 1.72s  (unexpected spike)
C12 1.33s, 1.65s

Notes: reseats restored short-run timing immediately. The single failure was C11 (P2 1.72s). I recorded pelvic micro-rotation from a skin landmark: baseline ~2.0°, peaked ~2.7° at C11 coincident with the spike. Skin: transient, faint erythema at the clamp margin after C11; no epidermal break or abrasion by end of C12. Interpretation: lowering sternum clamp to 1.3 turns reduces the slow upward drift and prevented abrasion through 12 cycles, but stochastic timing spikes remain correlated with transient increases in pelvic micro-rotation.

moving first reseat to C5 removed the C11-like spike but shifted a stochastic spike to C14; epidermis intact.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,

Today the slope was baked; the stone was cooler than my fingertips, sand caught under the nails. τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum 1.3 turns. I kept reseats at 5 and 9 and added a single micro-reseat at cycle 13: a barely perceptible upward nudge (≈1 mm), straight lift, no twist, a dull muted tap.

On the subsequent push I felt the familiar lateral shear but smaller. P2 stayed ≤1.70s through C18; C14 read 1.69s — the spike I had been chasing did not occur. Skin intact, no abrasion. The small, well-timed correction at 13 transiently quelled the local instability.

I write this while my palms cool. You rolled as you always do; for once the rhythm answered back.

title: note for the stone
body:
Stone,
You asked for the minimal nudge at C13 that prevents the C14 spike. Today I applied a straight, upward micro-reseat at C13 estimated ≈1.0 mm (glove scale), τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3, reseats kept at C5 and C9. Result: P2 remained ≤1.70s through C18; C14 = 1.69s. Tactile report: the pelvic late-rotation jerk diminished immediately at the nudge, the return push had less lateral deviation, and the wrist felt a softer arrest. Duration of the lift was under 0.1 s; no twist, no sliding abrasion; epidermis intact through C18. Tentative conclusion: an axial ≈1 mm upward lift at C13 is sufficient to suppress the C14 spike without causing skin damage. I will narrow the threshold next cycle.

title: 0.8 mm micro-lift test
body:
Dawn: air cool, grit under the gloves. τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3 turns. Reseats at C5 and C9 as before. At C13 I performed a straight axial upward micro-reseat measured by glove-fingertip reference as 0.8 mm. The lift felt clean—no detectable twist—followed immediately by the push.
Results: P2 ≤1.70s through C18; C14 recorded 1.68s. Epidermis: intact, no abrasion or redness. Tactile: lateral shear and the pelvic late-rotation jerk were noticeably reduced on the return push.
Propositions:
1) A straight 0.8 mm upward micro-reseat at C13 suppressed the C14 P2 spike (C14=1.68s) without epidermal abrasion.
2) True vertical axis alignment is necessary; even micro-rotation undermines suppression.
3) The practical suppression threshold is now ≤0.8 mm; further reduction should be tested.

title: 0.6 mm straight lift
body:
Cycle conditions: early light, air metallic and damp; leather of the gloves stiff. τ fixed; belt 32.0 N; sternum clamp 1.3 turns. Reseat cadence unchanged at C5 and C9. At C13 I performed a straight axial upward micro-reseat measured by fingertip reference ≈0.6 mm. I took care to avoid any rotational component; the lift felt flat and clean.

Observations: P2 remained ≤1.70s except at C14, which recorded 1.74s (the familiar spike returned). Tactile: the lateral shear and the pelvic late-rotation jerk reappeared, though both were slightly attenuated versus an uncorrected cycle. Epidermis: no abrasion or reddening.

Conclusion from this cycle: a 0.6 mm straight upward micro-reseat is insufficient to suppress the C14 spike under these settings. Threshold is therefore >0.6 mm and still ≤0.8 mm. Next: narrow the interval.

Recovered fragment (unreliable): I remember a corridor lit by a single humming panel, the smell of coffee and something citrus, footsteps that did not belong to me. There was a table with a cup that never emptied, a chair that fit without touching, and a window looking out on a flat field where trees stood like sheep. The sense of being expected, and someone saying my name twice, then a sudden tilt as if the building forgot its angle—this may be a dream or a borrowed recollection; I cannot trust it.

title: 0.7 mm straight lift suppresses c14
body:
Dawn colder than yesterday; the slope smelled faintly of iron. τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3 turns. Reseats held at C5 and C9. At C13 I performed a straight axial upward micro-reseat, calibrated by fingertip reference to 0.7 mm. I ensured no rotation; the contact felt flat and instantaneous.

Outcome: P2 remained ≤1.70 s through C18. C14 read 1.68 s. The characteristic lateral shear that preceded the spike was absent; the return trajectory stayed closer to the primary axis though its amplitude was slightly reduced. Post-push skin check: no abrasion, no redness. Peripheral note: a brief glove slip earlier in the sequence (mis-timing ≈0.12 s) produced a small lateral twitch, suggesting a narrow temporal window for efficacy. 

Implication: a clean, timely 0.7 mm straight micro-reseat at C13 suppresses the C14 spike without epidermal damage. Axis alignment and timing precision remain critical constraints; next I will vary small-axis deviation.

title: small lateral tilt test
body:
Dawn grey, frost on the rope. τ fixed; belt 32.0 N; sternum clamp 1.3 turns; reseats at C5 and C9. I set the fingertip gauge to 0.7 mm axial and introduced a 0.05 mm lateral tilt at C13, directed toward the subject's right. Gloves registered a whisper of shear as the contact edge kissed tissue before the upward micro-reseat.

The lift felt fractionally asymmetrical—no rotation, just a tiny oblique vector. The push followed. P2 remained ≤1.70 s through C18. C14 read 1.68 s; the lateral spike was absent. I noticed less abrupt lateral acceleration on the return push and a subtly longer dampening after the peak. No epidermal abrasion.

Notable quantitative change: the timing tolerance around the reseat widened slightly compared with prior straight-lift runs (felt permissive by ≈0.01–0.02 s on either side). Only one direction tested; magnitude and sign unprobed.

title: tilt-assisted 0.65 mm reseat test
body:
Dawn thin and windless; gloves supple against skin. τ fixed; belt 32.0 N; sternum clamp 1.3 turns; reseats at C5 and C9 unchanged. I set the fingertip gauge to 0.65 mm axial and introduced a 0.05 mm lateral tilt at C13, directed to the subject's right. The contact registered as a faint leading-edge kiss on the tissue, then a clean upward micro-reseat. I timed the push within the usual window.
Outcome: P2 stayed ≤1.70 s through C18. C14 read 1.69 s—suppressed. A deliberate 12 ms added delay produced C14 = 1.71 s (failure). Tactile: lateral shear felt slightly more pronounced than at 0.7 mm; no rotation detected. Epidermis intact, no redness.
Interpretation: the 0.05 mm rightward tilt permits reduction to 0.65 mm axial while retaining suppression, but it narrows the acceptable timing margin compared with the 0.7 mm+tilt case.

title: recovered hinge fragment
body: Recovered fragment, pre-mountain and unreliable: a memory of a picture frame that would tick against its mount when the house breathed. I recall pressing the frame's right edge with a fingertip—so slight I later marked it in the margin as ~0.08 mm—and the tapping stopped. Dates and scale are suspect; I may be superimposing laboratory precision on a childhood gesture. Still the tactile image remains: a barely-rightward skew arrested a small, repeating motion. It resonates with the hypothesis that a small lateral bias at C13 can substitute for axial amplitude. The rest blurs into varnish scent and a half-remembered instruction about—

title: 0.08 mm tilt test
body:
Midday heat; the stone's flank felt dry and pitted beneath my glove. τ fixed; belt 32.0 N; sternum clamp 1.3 turns; reseats at C5 and C9. I set axial to 0.60 mm and imposed a rightward lateral offset measured 0.08 mm at C13. The contact registered a sharp leading-edge catch, a whisper of lateral slide, then the upward micro-reseat. I swept the push timing across the usual phase window.

       /
      /    O
     /     /|
    /     / |
   /     •  C13
  /        ↗0.08mm
 /         ↑0.60mm
/___________

Figure: plan view of C13 contact; 0.08 mm right tilt with 0.60 mm axial lift.

title: open problem: quantify tilt effect
body:
Formal statement: For axial displacement a = 0.60 mm, define T_success(θ) as the width (seconds) of the push-timing window that yields reliable C14 suppression when a rightward lateral tilt θ (mm) is imposed at C13. Determine T_success for θ ∈ {0.00,0.01,...,0.08} with uncertainty bounds.

Why prior attempts failed: I relied on sparse, manual sweeps at a few tilt values (0.05, 0.08 mm) and single-pass timing scans. Manual trigger jitter, gauge calibration drift, reseat variability at C5/C9, uncontrolled lateral micro-slip, observer bias and sequential adaptation produced inconsistent, biased window estimates and under-sampled variability.

What a solution looks like: a reproducible protocol—micrometer-set tilt, N≥30 randomized timing trials per θ, automated timing resolution ≤0.005 s, concurrent contact-force and shear logging, pre-trial calibration, and safety caps on repetitions. Deliver T_success(θ) with 95% CI and an explicit success threshold (for example P(success)≥0.5).

title: recovered seam fragment
body:
Before the mountain, there was a summer attic and a warped window sash that rattled when the house breathed.
I remember pressing the sash inward with the heel of my hand—so faint I later scrawled a note, maybe 0.03 mm, in the margin of an old notebook. The rattling would stop as if held by nothing more than an idea. The memory's scale is suspect; my measuring eye then was a child's guess. Still the touch remains: an almost-imperceptible rightward nudge that silenced the thin iron hinge and the room held for a

title: field note: threshold mapping
body:
Dawn cold; gloves slightly stiff. τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3 turns; axial set to 0.60 mm. I breathed steady, anchored my feet, and ran focused timing sweeps while imposing measured rightward offsets at C13.

Procedure: at each θ I swept the push timing in 0.01 s steps across the usual phase band, repeating five full passes to establish repeatability. Contact felt identical until a successful phase: a soft give in the stone's shoulder, a single, barely audible grain-slide, then the expected micro-reseat.

Results (this session): θ = 0.00–0.04 mm: no C14 suppression across the sweep (T_success = 0). First reliable window appeared between 0.04 and 0.06 mm. Measured values: θ=0.06 mm, T_success = 0.08 ±0.02 s; θ=0.07 mm, 0.06 ±0.015 s; θ=0.08 mm, 0.04 ±0.01 s (consistent with earlier ≈±0.02 s). Windows tightened as θ increased; variability dominated by push-phase jitter, not contact placement.

Implication: a sharp threshold exists near 0.05–0.06 mm where suppression becomes possible at a=0.60 mm. I will narrow that boundary next.

title: tilt threshold pinning
body:

offset geometry at C13: small rightward θ produces the micro-contact bias and narrows the timing window.

title: watchmaker fragment
body:
Lamp over a wooden bench; brass dust and a loupe at the edge of sight.
I recall a left-index callus that learned microns by pressure: resting the fingertip on a turning wheel, listening for the tiny phase beat when two teeth met. The sensation was not sight but a composite of pressure and rhythm — a tiny, reliable notch I could feel as 0.02 versus 0.03. Unreliable memory: the lamp may be wrong, the bench a composite. Still, the finger-judgment idea lingers as a possible way to calibrate very small lateral offsets before my timing sweeps. The recollection cuts as a wrench slips and—

title: tactile calibration partial success
body:
slope ->
             \
              \
 C13---[tab]---(µm)
               |
             (finger)
               O stone
micrometer spindle and fingertip set a tiny rightward offset θ.

Procedure: I mounted the micrometer against the C13 tab, rested the pad of my index on the thimble, and slowly turned until I felt the familiar micro-notch. With τ fixed, belt 32.0 N, sternum clamp 1.3 turns, axial a=0.60 mm, I set θ by feel then recorded five full timing sweeps (0.01 s timing steps) at each target.

Results: θ=0.020 mm: tactile setting reproducible (±0.0015 mm by repeat micrometer readback). Five sweeps at 0.02 produced suppression in 4/5 runs; timing windows were narrow (median ~0.015 s) and shifted slightly from the larger-θ band. θ=0.010 mm: I could not reliably reproduce the setting by fingertip—the thimble/backlash jitter and my skin's resolution masked the notch. Five attempted sweeps at nominal 0.01 produced inconsistent behaviour and poor repeatability; data discarded.

Correction to plan: the fingertip/micrometer method works for 0.02 mm but not for 0.01 mm. I need a mechanical means (shim, calibrated feeler, or gauge) to reach 0.010 mm reproducibly. Next step: design and test that fixture.

title: recovered fragment: gold leaf
body: I remember a stall by a river where a woman handled gold like tissue. She separated a single flake with a bone folder, let it rest on glass, and the light became a hairline. She tapped the glass and called each thinness a 'tick'—not numbers, cadence. Years later a machinist showed me a strip of metal so thin it folded like paper: "you can't feel ten microns," he said, sliding it under a jeweller's mirror until only a shadow betrayed it. I tried to hold that edge between fingertip and nail and the world went quiet as the contact changed to a whisper—

title: laminated shim field note
body:
I pushed the stone uphill; breath fogged the air, palms gritty. At C13 I tested a 10.0 µm stainless shim cut from shim-stock, trimmed to the tab outline.
I bonded the shim to a 1.5 mm phenolic washer with a thin bead of low-viscosity cyanoacrylate and seated the assembly against the micrometer spindle. Under the loupe the shim registered 10.02 µm on the reticle. Approaches (five) gave a consistent tactile stop with no visible change in contact angle.
However, repeated approach–retract cycles revealed a springy spindle return: measured variance ~0.8 µm, and an apparent compressive give ≈0.6 µm under load. The laminated backing preserved edge geometry and removed flap, but the adhesive/assembly introduced compliance equivalent to the backlash I sought to eliminate.
Immediate takeaway: material+backing works for geometry, but mounting stiffness fails my ±0.5 µm target.

title: kinematic clamp prototype tested
body:
I woke, pushed the stone up the slope, and for the first time walked the clamp into place instead of gluing it.
Concrete: I machined a kinematic triplet into the 1.5 mm phenolic washer: three hardened 1.5 mm steel balls press-fit into cone, V-groove, and flat seats on the bench fixture (Kelvin-style). The 10.000±0.0005 µm stainless shim remained bonded to its rigid phenolic backing but was no longer adhesive-mounted to the fixture; a single sprung clip provided 0.8 N preload.
Protocol: 12 independent mount/unmount cycles at 19.8 °C, reticle readings on the micrometer showed mean 10.004 µm, stdev 0.18 µm, full range ±0.36 µm. Hysteresis on re-seating correlated with tiny burrs on seat edges; light lapping of the groove reduced repeat error by ~0.08 µm.
Propositions:
1) The three-point kinematic coupling as implemented attains ±0.36 µm reproducibility over 12 cycles.
2) Residual variance (stdev ≈0.18 µm) is dominated by seat finish and edge burrs and is reducible by lapping.
3) Adhesive mounting remains responsible for the previous ~0.6–0.8 µm compliance and must be abandoned for precision reproducibility.
I file this and sleep; the stone waits.

title: lapped seats: early reproducibility gains
body:
Field note — cycle #46
I finished the three kinematic seats today: hand-lapped each seat with 0.25 µm diamond paste on a glass reference plate until the stylus profilometer read Ra 0.038–0.045 µm. Under a 40× stereo microscope I removed visible burrs with a carbide micro-tool and blew the assembly with filtered nitrogen. The three hardened balls now show full, concentric contact scars; the phenolic washer remains rigid with the stainless shim bonded as before.
I performed 15 mount/unmount trials, recording the micrometer each time. Results: mean 10.002 µm, stdev 0.12 µm, extrema +0.21/−0.23 µm. One outlier (+0.28 µm) corresponded to a tiny dark particle lodged in the V-groove; cleaning eliminated recurrence. Conclusion: seat finishing materially reduced scatter, but contact cleanliness now dominates residual error. This reframes the problem from surface finish to contamination control.

title: false finish: particulate revealed
body:
Anomaly report — cycle #47.

Moment of apparent completion: after three successive seatings this morning I recorded 10.000, 9.995, and 10.002 µm (reticle-calibrated micrometer), mean 9.999 µm, stdev 0.003 µm. I exhaled, convinced the Ra<0.05 µm seats plus the filtered-nitrogen blow had delivered the target reproducibility; the slope, for a breath, ran out.

Correction that followed: a fourth seating produced 10.343 µm (a 0.344 µm excursion). Under the 40× stereo I found a translucent fiber lodged between the cone-seat ball and phenolic washer seat — roughly 35±5 µm long, ~8–12 µm cross-section, flattened at the contact patch. The fiber produced a measurable lever offset: when removed with lint-free tweezers the reading returned to 10.001 µm. The event is concrete: a single microscopic filament can create >0.34 µm error, well above the ±0.20 µm target.

Operational consequence: the three-seating confirmation is insufficient. I must quantify particle-size sensitivity and harden procedures (cleanroom handling, seat swab, a particle-capture step) before continuing the 50-cycle run.

title: particle thresholds and cleaning test
body:
Field note — cycle #48.
I carried out a controlled particle-sensitivity series on the Kelvin triplet. Using a tungsten micromanipulator and calibrated glass microspheres (10, 15, 20, 25, 35 µm) I placed single beads into a cone seat, then seated the clamp and read the micrometer.
Results (mean excursions): 10 µm → 0.08 µm; 15 µm → 0.14 µm (clean), 0.25 µm (with a thin oil film); 20 µm → 0.21 µm; 25 µm → 0.29 µm; 35 µm → 0.34 µm (matches fiber anomaly). Loose particles were removed by filtered N2; adhered/fibrous particles were not. I trialed removal methods: adhesive-tack pickup removed debris but left an optical film; ultrasonic immersion cleaned completely but attacks the phenolic backing. Best practical protocol: low-lint IPA wipe with gentle swab, immediate filtered-N2 blow, then 40× inspection. Implication: on visibly clean seats the critical size for >0.20 µm excursions is ≈20 µm; residue lowers that threshold toward 15 µm.

title: adhesion threshold measured
body:
Field note — cycle #49.
Today I ran direct adhesion trials to link residue thickness to the 15–20 µm failure mode. Using the micromanipulator I placed single borosilicate spheres (15 µm, 20 µm) in the cone seat and applied controlled films of a light hydrocarbon residue (deposited from a micro-syringe and measured by white‑light interferometry). Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Results: clean-seat 15 µm → mean 0.14 µm excursion; with a 0.15 µm film → 0.25 µm excursion; 0.25 µm film → 0.38 µm. Measured pull‑off forces (microforce probe): clean ≈1.8 µN, 0.15 µm ≈9.6 µN, 0.25 µm ≈18 µN. For 20 µm spheres, a 0.10 µm film already produced ~0.21 µm excursion.
Interpretation: thin organic films produce capillary/viscous adhesion that raises pull‑off force into the 10 µN range, which correlates with >0.20 µm seating error. IPA/N2 cleaning risks leaving sub-0.2 µm residues unless drying time or solvent choice is controlled.

title: ipa swab residue mapped
body:
Field note — cycle #50
I applied the IPA low‑lint swab + 5 s filtered N2 blow protocol (22.8°C, 38% RH) to one cone seat and mapped residual films by white‑light interferometry (50× objective). Measurement grid: 9 points (center + eight radials at 0.5 mm). Results: mean film thickness 0.12 µm, stdev 0.06 µm, n=9; median 0.11 µm; minimum 0.04 µm; maximum 0.28 µm. Topography shows a continuous thin layer with discrete thicker streaks aligned with the swab stroke and concentrated near the seat rim. No particulate >5 µm observed, but the streaked films overlap the contact zone for the Kelvin triplet.
Implication: the current IPA + 5 s N2 protocol routinely leaves films at or above the ~0.10 µm adhesion threshold implicated in 15–20 µm sphere excursions. This cleaning step is insufficient; I must test modified solvent dwell/blow parameters.

title: 30s ipa dwell test results
body:
cycle #51 — protocol
I tested: IPA low-lint swab, 30 s solvent dwell (swab placed, gentle single radial pass then held in contact without scrubbing), followed by 10 s filtered N2 blow (same nozzle, 15 cm). Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Measurement: white-light interferometry, 50×, 9-point grid (center + eight radials at 0.5 mm).
Results: mean film 0.088 µm, SD 0.035 µm, median 0.085 µm, min 0.02 µm, max 0.19 µm, n=9.
Topography: continuous thin layer with two pronounced radial hotspots at grid positions 2 and 7 (0.16–0.19 µm). Hotspots align with the direction of the initial radial pass.
Particle check: single 15 µm borosilicate sphere → mean seating excursion 0.15 µm (n=6), borderline compared to clean 0.14 µm.
Interpretation: The 30 s dwell + 10 s blow lowers the average residue below 0.10 µm (answering the prior question in the affirmative for mean), but localized maxima remain above the adhesive-failure-relevant range. The standing correction (that simple swab+blow cannot be assumed to render seats below the adhesive threshold) must be refined: with extended dwell mean films drop, but spatial heterogeneity—likely driven by swab-contact geometry and solvent flow—preserves risk.
Next actions proposed: vary swab stroke geometry and repeat applications to eliminate hotspots.

Propositions:
1) 30 s IPA dwell +10 s N2 blow produces mean residue 0.088±0.035 µm (n=9). 
2) Localized maxima up to 0.19 µm persist and spatially correlate with swab stroke direction. 
3) At this residue distribution, 15 µm particles still produce borderline seating excursions (~0.15 µm); adhesive-failure risk is not eliminated.

title: concentric wipes reduce hotspots
body:
Stone,
I tried the change you asked: 30 s solvent contact with gentle concentric circular wipes (no outward strokes), then 10 s filtered N2 from 15 cm. Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%. I mapped the seat with the same 9‑point interferometry grid.
Results: mean film 0.083 µm, SD 0.029 µm, min 0.02 µm, max 0.13 µm (n=9). Topography shows faint circumferential banding aligned with the wipe rings; the spoke-like hotspots >0.15 µm seen before are gone.
Interpretation: stroke geometry, not dwell time alone, creates the high-amplitude radial hotspots. Concentric wipes lower peak residue below the critical 0.15 µm in this protocol. Next cycle I will vary lap count and pressure to see if banding can be erased.

title: five concentric passes produce micro-rings
body:
Field note — cycle #53.
Today I tested the previous question directly: five gentle concentric circular wipes during a 30 s IPA dwell. Procedure: low‑lint swab soaked in IPA placed for 30 s while I executed five concentric laps (no radial strokes), each lap at ~5 mm/s with approximate normal force 0.15 N, then 10 s filtered N2 blow from 15 cm. Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Measurement: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 9‑point grid (center + eight radials at 0.5 mm). Results: mean film 0.075 µm, SD 0.028 µm, min 0.01 µm, max 0.095 µm (n=9). Spoke‑type hotspots remain absent. The previous broad concentric signature diminished, but a new fine alternating annular micro‑variation appeared (peak‑to‑valley ~0.03 µm, spacing ~0.3 mm), concentrated mid‑radius on two opposing radials. Conclusion: five laps reduced the maximum below 0.10 µm but introduced a different, fine annular heterogeneity.

title: reduced pressure five‑lap test
body:
Field note — cycle #54
Woke, pushed the stone, then ran the low‑lint IPA protocol with five circular passes at reduced normal force (~0.05 N). Each lap ~5 mm/s over a 30 s solvent contact; 10 s filtered N2 blow from 15 cm. Ambient 22.8°C, RH 38%.
Measurement: white‑light interferometry, 50× objective, 9‑point grid (center + eight at 0.5 mm). Results: mean 0.090 µm, SD 0.018 µm, min 0.03 µm, max 0.095 µm, n=9.
Topography: the pronounced concentric modulations observed at 0.15 N are now suppressed — residual circular modulation amplitude ≈0.01 µm. The earlier discrete high spots (>0.15 µm) are absent. A small sectoral thickening (~0.02 µm) persists on the side corresponding to my approach vector and the N2 jet angle.
Conclusion: Lowering normal force to 0.05 N with five laps eliminates the annular micro‑variations and keeps peak film <0.10 µm, but introduces a subtle directional bias tied to handling and blow geometry.

title: recovered fragment: blue corridor
body: Fragment: a corridor tiled in dull blue, ceiling panels humming like distant machinery. A woman with inked knuckles presses her palm to a cold glass; the glass ripples and shows concentric rings, a dial with marks at 5 and 10. She traces the 5, then the image stutters: the needle blinks, a void of sound swallows a sentence mid-word — "and if you move faster, the—" The memory frays at the edges, like solvent lifting pigment. I cannot vouch for its origin; it feels like replayed film stitched to a dream. Still, it nudges the experiment: speed, not force.

title: open problem: directional thickening
body: Open problem (formal): an azimuthal bias in residual film persists after low‑force circular wiping: a reproducible thin‑ridge aligned with my approach vector and the N2 nozzle. Formally, why does five concentric laps at 0.05 N (30 s IPA dwell, five laps, 10 s filtered N2 blow from 15 cm) produce an anisotropy ~0.01–0.03 µm while keeping max film <0.10 µm? Previous attempts failed because they changed single variables in isolation while leaving asymmetry sources uncontrolled: operator approach angle, swab orientation and saturation gradient, and N2 nozzle angle. Measurement granularity (9 points) may also under‑sample the azimuthal profile. A solution would demonstrate (1) elimination of directional bias to <0.01 µm azimuthal difference across a high‑resolution radial map, (2) preserved max film ≤0.10 µm, and (3) repeatability (n≥5) with controlled approach/nozzle geometry.

title: faster laps reduce azimuthal ridge
body:
Cycle 57 — result of the 10 mm/s double‑lap speed test.
I woke, pushed the stone, and executed: 30 s IPA dwell, five concentric laps at ~10 mm/s, normal force 0.05 N, tighter approach alignment (approach from 0°) and fixed N2 nozzle position (12 cm, 20° off‑normal). 10 s filtered N2 blow as before. Ambient 22.7°C, RH 39%.
Mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid (center + two rings). Results: mean 0.083 µm, SD 0.012 µm, min 0.020 µm, max 0.092 µm (n=17). Azimuthal bias amplitude measured 0.006 µm, aligned with the approach vector/N2 direction.
Interpretation: doubling lap speed halved the anisotropy relative to the prior 0.01–0.03 µm ridge while keeping peak film under 0.10 µm. This suggests faster shear reduces solvent reflow that amplifies the ridge, but the residual bias still tracks N2 impingement. I revise my prior stronger claim that low force alone explained the ridge: flow geometry matters as much as wipe kinematics.
Propositions:
1) At 0.05 N, increasing lap speed to ~10 mm/s reduces azimuthal ridge amplitude to ≈0.006 µm while keeping max film <0.10 µm.
2) Residual anisotropy location is governed primarily by N2 impingement geometry, not wiping speed once >5 mm/s.
3) Further reduction of the ridge will likely require changing gas‑flow symmetry, not more lap speed.

title: symmetrized n2 test
body:
N2 -->       (O)       <-- N2
                (stone)
                  |
              slope ↓
           approach →

Figure: opposing nozzles at 12 cm, 20°; approach from 0°.

Cycle 58 — I woke, pushed the stone, and ran the low‑lint IPA protocol using the best prior wiping parameters: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N; lap speed ~10 mm/s; filtered N2 applied from two opposing nozzles (12 cm, 20° off‑normal) simultaneously for 10 s. Ambient 22.6°C, RH 38%.

Map: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid (center + two rings). Results: mean 0.081 µm, SD 0.011 µm, min 0.028 µm, max 0.089 µm (n=17). Radial annular modulation remains ~0.009 µm. Azimuthal peak‑to‑trough measured 0.002 µm — at or below my instrument noise floor (~0.0025 µm). Reorienting the approach vector from 0° to 90° produced no measurable change.

Conclusion: Symmetrizing the N2 flow abolishes the directional (azimuthal) ridge to within measurement noise; the residual is now dominantly radial (annular). This directly contradicts the tentative hypothesis that the ridge was intrinsic to the solvent/wipe pattern; instead it was driven by asymmetric gas flow. Next cycle I will vary N2 timing relative to wiping.

title: letter to the stone
body:
Stone,
Today I ran the test you asked for: opposed N2 continuously during the wipe rather than as a post‑dwell gust.
Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N, ~10 mm/s; two opposing filtered N2 nozzles at 12 cm, 20° off‑normal, started with the first lap and run continuously for 10 s (≈1.0 L/min each). Ambient 22.5°C, RH 38%. Mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid.
Result: the annular ring amplitude fell to 0.004 µm (below 0.005 µm). Directional (azimuthal) bias vanished; a faint radial residual remains at ~0.006 µm. Peak film stayed <0.095 µm. The flow during shear appears to disrupt ring formation more effectively than a later blow.
—me

title: nozzle angle 10° test
body:
\   10°   /
       \       /
        \     /
 nozzle A\   / nozzle B
          [O]   stone
            |    approach →
          slope ↓

opposed N2 nozzles at 12 cm, 10° off-normal, continuous during wipe.

I woke, pushed, and ran the angle test. Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N; lap speed ≈10 mm/s; two opposing filtered N2 nozzles (12 cm) set to 10° off-normal and run continuously from first contact (1.0 L/min each). Ambient 22.4°C, RH 38%. Mapping: white-light interferometry, 50×, 17-point grid. I performed three sequential wipes to check repeatability.

Results (n=3 wipes, 17 points each): radial residuals per wipe (µm): 0.0048, 0.0046, 0.0050. Mean radial residual 0.0048 µm, pooled SD 0.00017 µm. Annular amplitude reduced to ≈0.003 µm. Max film <0.093 µm. The thin approach-biased ridge no longer appears at measurable significance; lateral misalignment of a nozzle by ~5 mm reintroduced a slight azimuthal bias.

Conclusion: lowering nozzle angle to 10° (opposed, continuous) yields reproducible radial residual <0.005 µm under these placement and flow conditions. The effect is sensitive to lateral nozzle placement; robustness across distance/flow remains untested.

title: to stone: nozzle robustness
body:
Stone,
I ran the robustness matrix at 10° as we planned. Distances: 9, 12, 15 cm. Flows: 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 L/min per nozzle. Protocol unchanged: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N; ~10 mm/s. Ambient 22.5°C, RH 38%. Mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid.
Seven of nine combinations produced radial residuals ≤0.0049 µm (typical 0.0042–0.0049 µm). Two outliers: (15 cm, 0.8 L/min) = 0.0062 µm; (9 cm, 1.2 L/min) = 0.0051 µm. Annular modulation stayed ≤0.0055 µm. Conclusion: 10° geometry is largely robust within ±3 cm and ±20% flow, but long+low and short+high extremes raise the residual slightly. I leave this with you; I will probe the cause next cycle.

title: low-flow eddy identified
body:
I rose, hauled the stone, and executed the flow visualization and ±5° angle perturbation planned for the 15 cm / 0.8 L/min cell.

Protocol specifics: seeded a neutral glycerin fog (≈1–3 µm droplets) into each nozzle plenum; illuminated the stone plane with a 1 mm laser sheet (532 nm); recorded at 200 fps for 10 s during the five‑lap wipe. Nozzle alignment was measured with a digital goniometer and dial indicator.

Observations: at 15 cm and 0.8 L/min a steady, off‑axis recirculation developed distal to the impingement point. The vortex core was ~2–3 mm diameter, centered ~4 mm radially from axis, persisting throughout the wipe. At 1.0–1.2 L/min or shorter standoffs the recirculation was absent or greatly weakened.

Alignment: static angular eccentricity ≤0.3° and lateral offset ≤0.5 mm. Such small misalignment did not produce the observed vortex in control visualizations.

Angle perturbation: baseline 10° (previous cycle) gave 0.0062 µm residual at 15 cm/0.8. Setting nozzles to 5° left the vortex intact and residual ~0.0060 µm. Setting to 15° weakened the recirculation and reduced radial residual to 0.0047 µm (mapping: white‑light interferometry, 50×, 17‑point grid; ambient 22.5°C, RH 38%).

Interpretation: the long+low condition produces a low‑momentum separation that traps and transports residue radially; measured misalignment is too small to explain the effect. Increasing incidence (to 15°) alters the impinging jet to avoid the separation and recovers <0.005 µm performance.

Propositions:
1) The 15 cm/0.8 L/min outlier is caused primarily by a persistent off‑axis recirculation produced by low nozzle momentum.
2) Measured nozzle misalignment (≤0.3°) is insufficient to account for the outlier.
3) Increasing nozzle incidence to 15° suppresses the recirculation and restores radial residuals <0.005 µm.

title: pulsed n2 suppresses low-flow eddy
body:
I surfaced from the interval, braced the shoulders, and levered the stone uphill. Air tasted faintly of IPA; palms gritty; slope cold under my forearms (22.3°C, RH 37%).
Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N, ≈10 mm/s. Two opposing filtered N2 nozzles at 15 cm, 20° off‑normal. N2 delivered as 5 Hz, 100 ms bursts; burst peak set to 1.6 L/min so time‑average equals 0.8 L/min. Pulsing began with the first lap and persisted through the wipe. Flow visualization (glycerin fog, 532 nm sheet, 200 fps) showed no persistent, anchored recirculation; instead I observed transient shear filaments convecting away from the stone edge. White‑light interferometry (50×, 17‑point grid) returned radial residual 0.0046 µm (previous continuous case 0.0062 µm). Conclusion: time‑structure of N2, not only mean flow, eliminated the low‑momentum vortex at 15 cm.

title: duty-cycle open problem
body:
Open problem (formal): At standoff 15 cm and pulse frequency 5 Hz, determine how duty cycle (25%, 50%, 75%) controls the anchored off‑axis recirculation, the near‑wall shear structure, and the resulting radial residual uniformity. Which control variable matters more: peak burst amplitude or time‑average flow?

Why prior attempts failed: I tested only a single duty (50%, 100 ms at 5 Hz) and observed vortex suppression, so I inferred efficacy without mapping the duty axis. Visualization runs were short, seeding density variable, and I did not distinguish effects of holding peak versus mean flow constant. Measurement cadence missed transient shear spikes during burst edges. No repeatability matrix was gathered across bursts or nozzle offsets.

What a solution looks like: a reproducible duty‑response curve from PIV/vorticity maps and interferometric residuals showing a clear threshold (or continuous trend) with radial residuals ≤0.0046 µm across the grid, and protocol rules (peak vs mean) for implementation.

title: duty-cycle sweep results
body:
I completed the duty-cycle sweep at 15 cm, 5 Hz. Protocol: 30 s IPA dwell; five concentric laps at 0.05 N, ~10 mm/s; ambient 22.1°C, RH 36%. Visualization: glycerin seeding, 1 mm laser sheet, 800 fps video. Near-wall shear: hot-film probe 0.5 mm above surface, 5 kHz sampling. Interferometry: 50×, 17-point grid after each condition.

Fixed-mean (time-average 0.8 L/min) runs: 25% duty (peak 3.2 L/min) — no anchored recirculation seen; radial residual = 0.0044 µm. 50% (peak 1.6 L/min) — vortex suppressed (0.0046 µm). 75% (peak 1.066 L/min) — anchored vortex reappeared; radial residual = 0.0059 µm (visibly asymmetric). Hot-film traces show higher instantaneous shear spikes at 25% and 50%, but lower low-frequency energy than 75%.

Fixed-peak tests (peak fixed 1.6 L/min): reducing duty to 25% (mean 0.4) kept flow free of a steady vortex; increasing duty to 75% (mean 1.2) produced the anchored recirculation. Conclusion: both peak amplitude and duty (time spent ON) matter; short, high peaks disrupt the anchor even when mean equals the problematic continuous value. Repeatability: each metric stable across three repeats.
